nameStory: Cape-ivy gets its name from its South African origins near the Cape of Good Hope, combined with its ivy-like climbing habit and heart-shaped leaves. Though it's not a true ivy at all, early settlers likely called it "ivy" because of how it scrambles up surfaces and spreads across the ground in similar fashion. The scientific name Delairea honors French botanist Delaère.
description: Cape-ivy is a climbing or trailing vine from South Africa that's part of the sunflower family, not the ivy family despite its name. It has soft, fleshy stems that can grow several feet long, scrambling over other plants or trailing along the ground. The heart-shaped leaves are bright green and somewhat succulent-feeling, while small yellow daisy-like flowers appear in clusters. This is an extremely rare escape in New England, with only one recorded observation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to ivy-like leaves that feel thick and slightly succulent when you touch them, with a waxy surface and prominent veining

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow daisy-like flowers in loose, branching clusters that smell sweetly fragrant, each about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Trailing or climbing vine with soft, fleshy stems that feel almost rubbery and break easily when bent

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green to purplish stems that are hollow and succulent-like, often rooting where they touch the ground

habitat: Cape-ivy is extremely rare in New England, likely found only as an occasional garden escape in coastal areas or around greenhouses. It would most likely appear in disturbed sites with mild microclimates, such as near heated buildings or in protected urban areas where it might survive brief cold snaps.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh bright green heart-shaped leaves on extending stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants are at their most vigorous, with trailing stems extending rapidly and small yellow flowers appearing in clusters.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in warm years, but plants begin to decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants are killed by freezing temperatures and would not survive New England winters outdoors.

funFact: Cape-ivy is such a successful invader in California that it can completely smother entire forest understories, but in New England it's so rare that there's only been one documented sighting — our cold winters are actually protecting us from this aggressive spreader!
confusionNotes: The heart-shaped leaves might remind you of true English ivy, but Cape-ivy's leaves are much more succulent and fleshy to the touch, and the yellow daisy flowers are a dead giveaway since true ivies have tiny greenish flowers. The waxy, thick leaf texture is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Cape-ivy belongs to the sunflower family (Asteraceae), not the ivy family (Araliaceae) at all. This is a classic case of common names being misleading — always look at those daisy-like flowers to remember it's actually related to dandelions and asters, not true ivies.
compareHints: Cape-ivy is the only member of the genus Delairea that escapes cultivation, so compare it instead to other trailing members of the sunflower family. Unlike groundsel or other Senecio species, Cape-ivy has distinctly heart-shaped, succulent leaves rather than deeply lobed or narrow leaves. The combination of trailing habit, yellow daisy flowers, and thick waxy heart-shaped leaves is unique among asters.
